In 1840 the Whig majority for Harrison was nearly 5000. It would be beyond reason to hope to overcome at once an army like that. We cannot afford to occupy our columns with incomplete returns, but will give the full result as soon as obtained. The Louisville Democrat of this day has the following:

THE ACCOUNT is—the hammer city should not haul down her colors. Under the most adverse circumstances the Whig majority has been reduced in this day to 600. Recurring to past returns, we find that in the Governor election exhibited the following fact: Leicher beat French, &c. Whole vote for Leicher 2000, and for French, 900. Now the majority for Whig, is 600; the entire vote being that of Whig, dem. 1840, which exhibits a Whig gain since 1840, of 1000, and a democratic gain of 500. And had not the honest Germans been excluded from the polls by brute force &c, the GAIN would have been 800 more, and the Whig majority 500 less.

The result from the interior, every way glorious so far as we have heard.

During the election in this city, the Whigs have been guilty of fraud, the most unblushing and deeds the most infamous. They have cast more than THREE HUNDRED AND FIFTY illegal votes IN the city, and the county of Jefferson. Men were permitted to vote who lived IN other States, having been brought here for that purpose. Many voted several times in the city and in the county; and in many instances, after they had taken their turns in voting here and in the county, they were shipped to other places. Money was raised by subscription for the aforesaid purpose of hiring knaves and thugs to beat honest citizens AND drive the foreign population from the polls. Even men of wealth, gave their interest in this cowardly and degrading purpose. Those hired ruffians were guilty of deeds the most shocking to humanity. No Germans could go to the polls in the last week without falling under the ire of the most heinous desperados. Multitudes on the first day of voting, were most cruelly beaten for no other reason than for going to vote. The moment a German was seen coming to the polls, these lied ruffians would immediately raise the cry, "There comes another damn black Dutchman"—and if he did not desist his transit out—and if he did not desist from presenting his vote, he would &c. suddenly be attacked with clubs, and beaten most shockingly. This horrible state of things continued during Monday, and was recommenced on Tuesday morning and continued until the close of the polls last evening. The consequence was, that over 1000 legal votes were kept OFF the polls. All this was done, yea, much more, in Louisville and in many instances in presence of officers who we've sworn to see that no violence was committed—that the law was observed. Yes, these alarming and cruel deeds were committed by those who make great professions of friendship for the Germans—by those who call themselves men. What a misnomer!

TIME American public has for long time
u been the victim of a false and dangerous
system of medicine founded on the practice of
LONG CONTINUED AND UNRELiEV-
ED PURGATION. The evils of this old
system are of the most widespread and alarm
ing character. They have reached through
every vein and artery Of our nation. In every
city, and village, and hanet-n every State
and Territory of our vast Republic, will be
found those who have suffered, or who are still
suffering from the injurious effects OF this old
system, Of whose practical utility the disease,
decay, and utter prostration of those who test
ii furnish the most condemning proofs!


COMMON DRASTIC PURGATION
scours out the system by the most improper
and violent means, and then leaves it, weak,
low, feeble, debilitated, TO regain its strength
as best it may. Sometimes the consequences
OF this old Purgalive practice are worse than
mere debility. Inflammation of the Bowels,
Slow Fever, Bloody Piles, and other horrible

HARRISBURG, April 5, 1844
SENATE.—Mr. Penniman, from the Committee on Banks, reported bill to extend the charter of the Carlisle Bank.


Mr. Sullivan, from the Committee on Corporations, reported bill to incorporate the Schuylkill County Cotton and Woolen Manufacturing Company.


On motion of Mr. Dimock, the Senate took up the bill relating to taxes on proceedings in Courts of Justice and in the Offices of Registers and Recorders. The bill underwent considerable discussion, and was postponed.


Mr. Champneys, from the Committee on Finance, reported, with amendments, House bill making appropriations for the expenses of Government.


The bill supplementary to the act abolishing Imprisonment for Debt, was called in its order and on it grew out a lengthy discussion. That part which repeals the portion of the act 1812, affecting debts contracted before its passage was stricken out and other amendments were made. The bill had progressed as far as the sixth section, when it was postponed.
The Dauphin Bank bill was next taken up and discussed till o'clock.
In the afternoon, the bill for the relief of Col. A. J. Pleasanton, passed with amendments. A supplement to the Charter of Mount Carbon and Port Carbon Railroad and supplement to the act incorporating the West Chester Railroad Company, each passed second reading.


HOUSE.—The bill providing for new Judicial district, to be composed of Schuylkill, Carbon and Monroe counties was taken up, and, after some time spent in discussion, the bill passed second and third readings. The vote on final passage stood 90 to 6.


The bill to extend the jurisdiction of Justice the Peace in certain cases, passed Committee of the Whole, and was referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.


The bill to reduce the capital stock of the Manufacturers and Mechanics Bank of Northern Liberties, passed second and third readings.


The Militia bill was taken up on second reading and discussed till the hour of adjournment. In the afternoon it was again resumed, and passed second reading after lengthy discussion. On the vote to transcribe for third reading, the yeas were 55 nays 80.

Mississippi relieved from the oppressive taxation system, which is extremely more grinding and oppressive to the great body of the people, than if we were to pay them just safeguards.

The taxation system of this state is as flawed as can be described. In my opinion, the present system of taxation on property accords no more with the principles of justice than any other too. A government protects every species of property and value, whether such property has real or ideal value; it would seem, requires that every species of property, properly considered, under the protection of a humane government, should contribute according to its usage to the support of the government which protects it. The greater portion of the property in the state subject to taxation is taxed according to this principle, but a portion is taxed by different modes, and operations very considerable in value are not taxed at all. All negro slaves between five and sixty years of age are taxed the same, whether of the same value or not; and negro slaves under five years of age and over sixty are exempt from taxation. Lands and or furniture of great value are not subjected by the present law to any tax whatever. I would recommend a resort to objects of taxation, and would include as such new objects negro slaves under the age of five years, and every description of household furniture, and every other species of property of either real or ideal value. I would tax each species of property according to its value. I imagine this would augment the revenue of the state considerably.

Ultimately connected with the finances of the state is the subject of the reduction of the expenses of the state. In contemplating the expenses of the different departments of the state government, I find no expenditure connected with the executive or legislative departments, which appear to be very moderate. When we turn our attention to the judicial department, we find that the administration of public justice costs the people of the state a vast sum annually in expenditure on account of the judicial department of the government of the state, or salaries of officers alone, which amounts to sum reaching near the amount of $10,000 per annum. This, in my opinion, is greater expenditure than the public service in this department requires a salary. If in this department salaries were reduced at least one-third without detriment to the public service.

For the purpose and as a mode of reduction, I would suggest the propriety of arranging the constitution in such manner as to abolish the office of the sergeant at law, and confer Chancery jurisdiction on the circuit courts. I would recommend the repeal of the law establishing the Vice Chancery Court and the reduction of the number of judicial districts to even at most. This would increase the labors of the circuit court judges; as their labors would be greatly increased, I am inclined to the opinion that justice and the faithful administrator of that branch of the public service would require their salaries to be increased to $3,000 per annum; this, with the reduction of the district attorneys to seven, would reduce the expenditures of this branch of the government for the salaries of judicial officers alone to an amount of between $20,000 and $30,000 per annum.

The last annual report of the inspectors of the penitentiary is herewith submitted for your consideration. The annual report of the inspectors for the year A.D. 1842 is lost or misplaced, which prevents me from submitting the same. Also, I would remark that these reports are extremely unsatisfactory, so far as relates to the financial affairs of the institution. The report of the year A.D. 1841 represented the institution as having made large profit to the state for that year, a sum between six and seven thousand dollars. The report herewith submitted represents the institution as having caused loss to the state for the year A.D. 1842 of upwards of $15,000. I do not hesitate to say that neither the former nor the latter is satisfactory.

Submitting for your consideration the letters of Allen M. as to the cost of machinery therein referred to, I would worthy of your serious consideration, whether the interest of the state would not be improved by the introduction of such machinery and the establishment of manufacturing in the state prison. Should you determine to introduce such machinery, a question of grave importance is whether it would be prudent to locate the institution at some point where water power to propel the machinery could be obtained—as also other necessary materials at cheaper rates than can now be obtained. I am inclined to the opinion that the institution is in a bad condition.

If the state should possess an institution which has possession of any other, I would suggest the power on the superintendent to appoint an assistant keeper, and other officers and guards except the inspectors. I am inclined to the opinion that the superintendent should be authorized by law to take bond and security, either to himself or to the state, from the assistant keeper, and all other officers, for the faithful performance of their duties, and to remove or dismiss them at pleasure upon finding them incompetent or unworthy.

There has been no material change in our foreign relations since my last Annual Message to Congress. With all the powers of Europe we continue on the most friendly terms. Indeed, it affords me much satisfaction to state, that a more tranquil peace of that enlightened and important quarter of the globe has ever been, apparently, more firmly established. The conviction that peace is the true policy of nations, would be growing and becoming deeper amongst the enlightened everywhere; and there is no people who have stronger interest in distinguishing the sentiments, and adopting the means of preserving and giving a permanence, than those of the United States. Amongst these, the first and most efficient are, no doubt, the strict observance of justice and the honest and punctual fulfillment of all engagements. But it is not to be forgotten that, in the present state of the world, it is less necessary to be ready to enforce their observance and fulfillment, in regard to ourselves, than to observe and fulfil them on our part, in regard to others.

Since the close of your last session, a negotiation has been formally entered upon between the Secretary of State and Her Britannic Majesty's Minister Plenipotentiary and Envoy Extraordinary resident at Washington, as to the rights of their respective nationals in and over the Oregon territory. That negotiation is still pending. Should it, during your session, be brought to a definite conclusion, the result will be promptly communicated to Congress; I would, however, again call your attention to the recommendations contained in previous messages, designed to protect and facilitate emigration to that territory. The establishment of military posts at suitable points upon the eastern line of land travel, would enable our citizens to migrate in comparative safety to the fertile regions below the falls of the Columbia, and make the provision of the existing convention for the lawful occupation of the territory by subjects of Great Britain, and the citizens of the United States, more available than heretofore to the latter.

These posts would continue places of rest for the weary emigrants, where he would be sheltered securely against the danger of attack from the Indians, and be enabled to recover from the exhaustion of a long line of travel. Legislative enactments should also be made which should spread over him the aegis of our laws, so as to afford protection to his person and property when he shall have reached his distant home. In this latter respect, the British Government has been much more careful in the interests of such of her people as are to be found in that country, than the United States. She has made necessary provision for their security and protection against the acts of those viciously disposed and lawless; and her emigrants repose in safety under the panoply of her laws. Whatever may be the result of the pending negotiation, such measures are necessary. It will afford me the greatest pleasure to witness a happy and favorable termination of the existing negotiation upon terms compatible with the public honor; and the best efforts of the Government will continue to be directed to this end.

I would have given me the highest satisfaction, in this, my last annual communication to Congress, to have been able to announce to you the complete and entire settlement and adjustment of other matters which were referred to in previous messages, the difference between the United States and the Government of Her Britannic Majesty. It is so obviously the interest of both countries, in respect to the large and valuable commerce which exists between them, that all causes of complaint, however inconsiderable, should be with the greatest promptitude removed—that it must be regarded as a cause of regret, that any unnecessary delays should be permitted to intervene. It is true that, in pecuniary point of view, the matters alluded to, are altogether insignificant in amount, when compared with the resources of that great nation; but nevertheless, more particularly this limited class which arise under seizures and detentions of American ships on the coast of Africa, upon the mistaken supposition indulged in all the time the wrong was committed, of their being engaged in the slave trade, deeply affecting the sensibilities of our Government and people. Great Britain, having recognised her responsibility to repair all such wrongs, by her action in other cases, leaves nothing to be regretted upon this subject as to all cases prior to the reign of Washington, and the delay in making suitable reparation in such of them plainly within the principle of others which she has long since adjusted, the injuries inflicted by delays in the settlement of these claims, fall with severity upon the individual claimants and makes a strong appearance of her magnanimity and sense of justice in speedy settlement. Other matters also in relation to the construction of existing treaties also remain unadjusted, and will continue to be brought under her attention.

It is our painful task to record, this afternoon, one of the most destructive gales ever visited the Western section of our State. The gale of Friday at Buffalo, as will be seen by the letter below and the extracts from The Commercial of Saturday evening.

BUFFALO, Oct. 7, 1844
All is ruin here. The terrific gale last night has crushed some forty houses in our city—East flooded all the stores between the canal and harbor, and all below the Terrace. Some forty dead bodies have been taken from the river, probably two hundred lives lost.

Every store in ruins, 21.2 feet water on my lower floor; some stores on the deck had six feet water in. Several steamboats, and vessels ashore—We know not what the loss on the lakes may be, but here it is immense.

"A large quantity of wheat and flour wet, of course. The only business here to-day is to look after the lives of sufferers.

A postscript to another letter says: Some fly dead bodies of men, women and children have been picked up among the ruins. No one can tell how many more will be added to the fatal list."

From the Buffalo Commercial of Saturday evening.

Last night we experienced a gale more violent and destructive than ever before known. The weather yesterday was cold and uncomfortable, with occasional drizzling showers of rain. Between nine and ten the wind veered to the South and warm heavy rain fell. At eleven the wind suddenly shifted to the North, and for about half an hour blew with great force, accompanied with rain. It then again changed to the South West—About midnight the gale commenced and raged like a hurricane; up to nearly four o'clock this morning, when its fury somewhat abated, but a heavy gale has continued to blow up to the hour of going to press.

The damage to property is immense, and the destruction is awful.

"WHEN IS THE TIME TO DIE?"

"When is the time to die?"
When the spring sky boundeth o'er us,
When the song of the bird
From the green woods is heard,
And the bright streams dance before us;
When the earth is laid and our heart is strong,
Let me pass away like the morning song.
"Then is the time to die."

When the lamp of the soul hath been lighted,
And like the dew on the rose died,
Is the bright repose,
Of affections pure and unblighted,
Softly breaks o'er the spirit. Oh bear me away,
Such glory is all too bright to stay.

"When is the time to die?"
When the rich, ripe summer gloweth,
Ere the soul grow faint,
And utter complaint,
Of the gifts kind heaven bestoweth,
With light around, and joy within,
Bear me away, ere the shades begin.

JOHN TYLER A WAR ON MEXICO.


The Tribune was the first paper this side of the Alleghanies to give the news that the Executive was moving troops from Missouri to the Sabine; and so extraordinary was the fact that it obtained very little credence. Now that it is established beyond doubt—confessed, indeed, the John Tyler has not only ordered two regiments to the Texan frontier, but in substance placed them under the orders of the President of Texas, backed by sending fleet to the harbor of Vera Cruz, with orders to oppose by force any American fleet sailing for the coast of Texas.

The Country is electrified. Stocks fell yesterday, and there was that general feeling of apprehension and insecurity which is the forerunner of War. This is no illusion—we are at this moment in imminent danger of War—a War undertaken in defiance of the opinion of the civilized world, and for objects which will subject us to general abhorrence—into which a step may precipitate us. For suppose Com. Conner shall take his position off the harbor of Vera Cruz, and Mexican fleet or single vessel of war shall see fit to weigh anchor and stand out, what is the consequence? Our Commander hails, and demands the destination of the Mexican. Of course, if the latter believes himself strong enough, he will answer that it is none of our business, or something like it; and then our Commander has no choice but to fire into him, which is War, or cover himself, his flag, his Nation with utter sal ridicule and disgrace. But suppose the Mexican force weak and its Commander answers that his destination is Cuba, or Carriha-gena, New Orleans, or anywhere else—can Com. Conner be satisfied with this? Must he not insist that the Mexican send his papers on board—that he furnish convincing evidence that he is not bound to Texas, and mediates no act of hostility against that region? Is not here the clearest National insult and humiliation? Is not here the most exasperating blockade of the chief port of Mexico? Make the case of Mexico of one, and suppose it were England which thus beleaguered New York, is there an officer in the American Navy who would submit to such an outrageous insult so long as he had guns on its carriage? Is there one man in our Navy who would not far sooner go to the bottom than face his countrymen after submitting to such degradation of the National ensign? He might strike his flag, indeed, to overwhelming force; but this is submitting to the fortunes of War—and War, it is clearly, is the moment our fleet has formed the blockade of Mexican ports.

Never this nation had cause to feel ashamed and to cover itself in the ashes of humility. That time has now arrived. In the midst of profound peace, the folly of our stupid, knavish President has, to all human probability, precipitated us into war, by the signature of his infamous name to an infamous treaty, made in the dark, with the most infamous of all renegades, Sam Houston. Mexico forsooth is dismembered, and the Federal fleets and armies are summoned there to maintain this wanton wrong and injury to a nation with which we have treaties of amity and peace. We have heard of kings that could do no wrong; but we, by the avenging dispensation of God, have a President who can do nothing but wrong. Will the nation—will Congress suffer this crime in the President to pass unrebuked, or will not Congress promptly impeach the traitor, and hurl him from that chair, which he and he only has ever disgraced with conduct, in comparison with which, the blackest treason is whiter than snow.
